summary: A summary listing of the RFCs numbered 1400 through 1499. It is a reference index, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of contents for one hundred small documents, so you can see what each one is about.

questions: what rfcs are in the 1400 series
subtitle: A reference guide to one hundred RFCs spanning networking, standards, and management.

tldr.problem: Finding information about the RFCs numbered 1400 through 1499 requires searching through individual documents spread across the RFC archive.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1499 collects a summary line and brief description for each of the 100 RFCs in this series, letting readers scan the purpose of each document in one place.
tldr.outcome: This index helps researchers and implementers quickly understand what work was done in this era of the RFC series, from the mid-1990s.

today: RFC 1499 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted, so it remains a valid reference guide to understanding the RFCs published in its range.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 1499 is a reference listing of the RFCs numbered 1400 through 1499, published by Josh Elliott of USC Information Sciences Institute in January 1997. Unlike protocol specifications, this memo does not define a standard. Instead, it provides a structured summary of what each of the one hundred RFCs in this range covers, serving as a status report on network standards and specifications issued during that period.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a simple list of what 100 other documents are about. It helps you find the right manual without reading all 100 of them.

sections.title: The RFCs 1400-1499
sections.content: The RFCs 1400 through 1499 span a diverse range of topics. Many are Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or Internet Standards on the standards track, including protocols for network management (the SNMPv2 suite), routing (AURP, IDPR, BGP/OSPF interaction), directory services (LDAP, X.500), and electronic mail (MIME, X.400 mappings). Others are informational RFCs covering topics like character sets, network administration tools, and experimental protocols. The memo notes that readers should consult the latest Internet Official Protocol Standards document for the current status of these RFCs, as standards may change after publication.
sections.plainLanguage: These 100 documents cover many topics: how to manage networks, how data travels between networks, how computers find each other, how to send email, and experimental ideas. Some became official standards, and others stayed experimental.

sections.title: Categories and Types
sections.content: The 100 RFCs break down into several categories. A significant subset are network management documents, centered on SNMPv2 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 2), which modernized how administrators monitor and control network devices. Routing documents describe protocols for directing packets across large networks, including AURP for AppleTalk networks and IDPR for policy-based routing. Directory services RFCs address how systems find other systems and their services. Electronic mail and related protocols make up another cluster, improving compatibility between different email systems. Character encoding RFCs address how different languages are represented on networks. Each entry includes the RFC number, author, publication date, title, and a one-paragraph description of its purpose and scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The documents fall into groups: how to run networks, how to send messages between networks, how to find computers by name, how to handle different languages, and experimental ideas people tried.

sections.title: How to Use This Summary
sections.content: Each RFC entry follows a consistent format: the RFC number, the author's name, publication date, and title, followed by a summary paragraph drawn from the RFC's abstract or status statement. Some RFCs are marked as STANDARDS-TRACK, indicating they are part of the Internet standards process and may advance in status. The memo reminds readers that the list reflects the status at publication time. For the most current status of any standard or proposal, the Internet Official Protocol Standards document (published by the Internet Architecture Board) provides authoritative information.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry tells you the document number, who wrote it, when it came out, what it is called, and what it does. Some documents are marked as standards that might become more official later on.
